title: Little Office of S. Aloysius Gonzaga of the Society of Jesus
translationNotice: English translation prepared for Sacrum Florilegium; not supplied in the source PDF.

blocks.source: ℣. Domine, labia mea aperies,
blocks.english: ℣. O Lord, open my lips,

blocks.source: ℟. Et os meum annunciabit laudem tuam.
blocks.english: ℟. And my mouth shall declare Thy praise.

blocks.source: Gonzaga, salve floscule Favore Virginali, Prognate flos tenellule De stirpe Principali Te luna Martis edidit, Te Martiale sidus; Orbique te concredidit Sol, cum teneret Idus.
blocks.english: Hail, Gonzaga, little flower blessed by the Virgin’s favour, tender blossom born of princely stock. The moon of Mars brought thee forth, the star of Mars; and the sun entrusted thee to the world when it held the Ides.
blocks.editorialNote: The earlier 1745 edition, p.283, confirms the printed lunar, Martian and Ides imagery. English preserves it without adding a birth date or an astrological interpretation. The attached Latin remains unchanged. The comparison uses the earlier 1745 edition, not the unexamined cited 1783 edition.

blocks.source: ℣. Dominus ab utero vocavit me.
blocks.english: ℣. The Lord called me from the womb.

blocks.source: ℟. Ergo judicium meum cum Domino, et opus meum cum Deo meo.
blocks.english: ℟. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.

blocks.source: Oremus,
blocks.english: Let us pray,

blocks.source: Deus, qui famulum tuum B. Aloysium ad majorem nominis tui gloriam in Societatem Filii tui vocare dignatus es: largiri quaesumus, ut, cujus angelicam puritatem veneramur in terris, ejus gloriae participes fieri mereamur in caelis. Per Dominum nostrum, etc.
blocks.english: O God, who didst deign to call Thy servant Blessed Aloysius into the Society of Thy Son for the greater glory of Thy name, grant, we beseech Thee, that we who venerate his angelic purity upon earth may be found worthy to share his glory in heaven. Through our Lord, etc.

blocks.source: ℣. Deus in adjutorium meum intende.
blocks.english: ℣. O God, come to my assistance.

blocks.source: ℟. Domine ad adjuvandum me festina. Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto.
blocks.english: ℟. O Lord, make haste to help me. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost.

blocks.source: Quem te vocabo vernulam Num tulipam colore? Violamne, veris gemmula, Casto fragrantem odore? Uterque flos est Virginis, Flos est uterque Flora Gonzaga tu propaginis Cujus flagras amore.
blocks.english: What spring blossom shall I call thee? A tulip for thy colour? Or a violet, little jewel of spring, fragrant with a chaste scent? Each is a flower of the Virgin, each a flower of Flora. Gonzaga, thou art of the stock with whose love thou burnest.
blocks.editorialNote: The earlier 1745 edition, p.284, prints the genitive “Florae”, corresponding to the attached “Flora”. The closing genitive “Propaginis” is retained as “of the stock”; the English no longer invents a masculine divine referent (“Him”). It preserves the relative wording and floral imagery without assigning an unstated identity to the stock. The attached Latin remains unchanged. The comparison uses the earlier 1745 edition, not the unexamined cited 1783 edition.
blocks.originalPreparedEnglish: What spring blossom shall I call thee? A tulip for thy colour? Or a violet, little jewel of spring, fragrant with a chaste scent? Each is a flower of the Virgin, each a flower of Flora. Gonzaga, thou art a shoot of Him with whose love thou burnest.

blocks.source: Gonzaga vix hunc hortulum Orbis subis, tenellis Mox sanctiorem flosculum Fers Numini labellis: Quando Mariam, et Jesulum Sic nominas biennis, Ut orbis in miraculum Oraveris triennis.
blocks.english: Gonzaga, scarcely dost thou enter this little garden of the world when from thy tender lips thou offerest a holier flower to God. At two years old thou namest Mary and little Jesus; at three thou prayest, to the wonder of the world.

blocks.source: Jesu, et Mariae literas De more tuliparum In cor tuum transmisseras:
blocks.english: Thou hadst carried the letters of Jesus and Mary into thy heart, after the manner of tulips:

blocks.source: Ut quinque litterarum Mox syllabas adnecteres, Illisque sanctiores; Orationes plecteres, Versusque castiores.
blocks.english: That thou mightest soon join the syllables of their five letters, and weave with them holier prayers and chaster verses.

blocks.source: Undene major paulum Hortum tuum colebas, Et suaviorum flosculum Cor ut daret, volebas? Quare supremo Numini Audes, sacraque Virgini Offerre puritatem.
blocks.english: A little older than eleven, thou didst tend thy garden, wishing thy heart to yield a sweeter little flower. Therefore thou darest offer purity to the Most High God and to the holy Virgin.
blocks.editorialNote: The earlier 1745 edition, p.285, prints “Undenne major paulum”: a little older than eleven. It also includes “Vovere castitatem” (to vow chastity), absent from the attached stanza; that extra line is not imported. The English specifies the age supported by the checked earlier reading. The attached Latin remains unchanged. The comparison uses the earlier 1745 edition, not the unexamined cited 1783 edition.
blocks.originalPreparedEnglish: A little older, thou didst tend thy garden, wishing thy heart to yield a sweeter little flower. Therefore thou darest offer purity to the Most High God and to the holy Virgin.

blocks.source: In serta vix haec planctula, In corde seminatur Gonzaga, et ore blandula Rosa inde procreatur Quae blandientis Cypridis Ne fraudibus pateret, Spernit jocos Adonidis, Ut castior lateret. Hinc tauricis, hinc funibus, Calcaribus, catenis Se se induit, ceu vepribus, Ut obviat venenis. Nec sat: cruore proprio Apud Patrem perorat? Jesuque sub tentorio Latere flos hic orat.
blocks.english: Scarcely is this little plant sown in the heart for garlands, Gonzaga, when a sweet rose springs from thy lips. That it might not fall prey to the wiles of alluring Cypris, it scorns the play of Adonis and hides in greater chastity. Hence he clothes himself with scourges of hide, with ropes, spurs, and chains, as though with thorns, to withstand poison. Nor is this enough: with his own blood he pleads before the Father; and this flower prays to hide beneath the tent of Jesus.

blocks.source: ℣. Ex omnibus floribus orbis elegisti tibi lilium unum.
blocks.english: ℣. From all the flowers of the world Thou hast chosen for Thyself one lily.

blocks.source: ℟. Lilium inter spinas.
blocks.english: ℟. A lily among thorns.

blocks.source: Transfertur ergo patria Gonzaga flos ab urbe, Romanae in Urbis atria: Sed saeviente sede In urbe pestilentia, Dum gnaviter ministrat Aegris, febris constantia Victus sub astra migrat.
blocks.english: Thus Gonzaga, the flower, is transplanted from his native city into the courts of Rome. But when pestilence rages foully in the city, while diligently ministering to the sick, overcome by persistent fever, he passes to the stars.
blocks.editorialNote: The earlier 1745 edition, p.285, prints “foede” (foully) rather than the attached “sede”. The English follows the checked earlier wording, describing pestilence raging foully in the city. The attached Latin remains unchanged. The comparison uses the earlier 1745 edition, not the unexamined cited 1783 edition.

blocks.english: ℣. Although I was free, I made myself the servant of all.

blocks.english: ℟. For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

blocks.source: Flos amice Numina O gemma Tuliparum! Infense flos cupidini Splendor, decus stolorum, O castitatis lilium Gonzaga! digne caelos; Da, da tuorum insignium Nos aestuare zelo: Da, da superna quaerere; Ridere cuncta vana; Terrena da contemnere; Vitare da profana.
blocks.english: O flower dear to the God, O jewel among tulips! O flower hostile to lust, splendour and honour of roses, O lily of chastity, Gonzaga, worthy of heaven! Grant, grant that we may burn with zeal for thy distinctions. Grant that we may seek heavenly things and laugh at all that is vain; grant that we may despise earthly things and shun what is profane.
blocks.editorialNote: The earlier 1745 edition, p.286, prints “Numini” and “rosarum”, corresponding to the attached “Numina” and “stolorum”. The English now follows that attested reading: a flower dear to God, splendour and glory of roses. The prior literal divine-powers and robes rendering is preserved in the review history. The attached Latin remains unchanged. The comparison uses the earlier 1745 edition, not the unexamined cited 1783 edition.
blocks.originalPreparedEnglish: O flower dear to the divine powers, O jewel among tulips! O flower hostile to lust, splendour and honour of robes, O lily of chastity, Gonzaga, worthy of heaven! Grant, grant that we may burn with zeal for thy distinctions. Grant that we may seek heavenly things and laugh at all that is vain; grant that we may despise earthly things and shun what is profane.

sourceReading.reading: Flos amice Numini; Splendor, decus rosarum!
